case.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (C. E. Shannon, 1948), Section 6 Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy
case.excerpt: 6. Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy. Suppose we have a set of possible events whose probabilities of occurrence are p_1, p_2, ..., p_n. These probabilities are known but that is all we know concerning which event will occur. Can we find a measure of how much "choice" is involved in the selection of the event, or of how uncertain we are of the outcome? If there is such a measure, say H(p_1, p_2, ..., p_n), it is reasonable to require of it the following properties: (1) H should be continuous in the p_i. (2) If all the p_i are equal, p_i = 1/n, then H should be a monotonic increasing function of n: with equally likely events there is more choice, or uncertainty, when there are more possible events. (3) If a choice be broken down into two successive choices, the original H should be the weighted sum of the individual values of H. Theorem 2: The only H satisfying the three above assumptions is of the form H = -K sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i log p_i, where K is a positive constant (it merely amounts to a choice of a unit of measure). Quantities of the form H = -sum p_i log p_i play a central role in information theory as measures of information, choice and uncertainty, and will be recognized as the entropy of statistical mechanics. With logarithms to the base 2, the unit is the bit. Properties of H: (1) H = 0 if and only if all the p_i but one are zero, this one having the value unity; thus only when we are certain of the outcome does H vanish, otherwise H is positive. (2) For a given n, H is a maximum and equal to log n when all the p_i are equal (i.e., 1/n); this is also intuitively the most uncertain situation. For two possibilities with probabilities p and q = 1 - p, H = -(p log p + q log q), which is plotted as a function of p in Fig. 7.
case.focus: Explain discrete entropy (Section 6, H = -sum p_i log2 p_i) using a small probability distribution. Let the learner change the distribution and the number of outcomes. Show probabilities, individual contributions, and total entropy in bits. Compare a certain outcome with equally likely outcomes. Check that certainty gives zero bits and four equally likely outcomes give two bits; handle zero probabilities correctly.
case.audience: Engineering undergraduate who knows basic probability and logarithms but has not studied information theory.

plan.concept: Discrete entropy H = -sum p_i log2 p_i as a measure of choice/uncertainty, with its two key properties (H=0 iff certain; H=log2 n when uniform).
plan.computation: Normalize the entered weights into a probability vector p_i; compute each contribution c_i = -p_i log2 p_i (with 0 log 0 = 0); sum to H; also compute the uniform reference log2 n and the maximum-contribution index.
plan.visual: Left: bar chart of p_i with the uniform level 1/n marked. Right: bar chart of contributions c_i stacked to show H, plus a horizontal reference line at log2 n.
plan.controls: n (number of outcomes, 1..6), a weight vector of length n (resized with n), and a preset selector for certain / uniform / skewed distributions.
plan.checks: H >= 0; H = 0 iff exactly one p_i = 1; H <= log2 n with equality iff all p_i equal; sum p_i = 1; sum c_i = H; zero probabilities contribute exactly 0.

spec.title: Entropy: How Much Choice Is in a Distribution?
spec.hook: You will build a small probability distribution and watch Shannon's entropy $H = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i$ count, in bits, how uncertain the outcome is.
spec.idea:
Shannon asks: given probabilities $p_1, \dots, p_n$ for a set of possible events, how much **choice** is involved in seeing which one occurs? He requires three things of any such measure $H$: it should be continuous in the $p_i$; it should increase with $n$ when all outcomes are equally likely; and breaking a choice into two successive choices should give the same total as one step. Theorem 2 says only one family of functions does this: $H = -K \sum_i p_i \log p_i$.

With $\log$ base 2 the constant $K$ just fixes the unit, and that unit is the **bit**. Each term $-p_i \log_2 p_i$ is that outcome's contribution: an outcome with tiny probability contributes little (it is rarely chosen), and an outcome with probability 1 contributes nothing (there is no choice at all).

Two properties make the formula easy to sanity-check. First, $H = 0$ exactly when one $p_i$ equals 1 and the rest are 0 — certainty means no uncertainty. Second, for fixed $n$, $H$ is largest when all $p_i = 1/n$, and then $H = \log_2 n$: two equally likely outcomes give 1 bit, four give 2 bits.

In the playground you set the number of outcomes and their weights. The weights are normalized into probabilities, so you can type any non-negative numbers and the page shows the resulting $p_i$, each contribution $-p_i \log_2 p_i$, and the total $H$.
spec.why: Entropy is the currency of information theory: it is the average number of bits needed to describe an outcome, and it is the limit that compression and coding schemes approach. It also gives engineers a single number for how spread out or peaked a distribution is, which is why it reappears in coding, machine learning and statistical physics.

equations.caption: Theorem 2: the only measure of choice satisfying Shannon's three requirements. $K$ is a positive constant that only sets the unit.
The same formula with base-2 logarithms and $K=1$; the unit is then the bit.

equations.tex: H = 0 \iff p_i = 1 \text{ for one } i, \; p_j = 0 \text{ otherwise}
equations.caption: Property (1): entropy vanishes exactly when the outcome is certain.

equations.tex: H \le \log_2 n, \quad H = \log_2 n \iff p_i = 1/n \; \forall i
equations.caption: Property (2): for fixed $n$ the maximum is $\log_2 n$, attained by the uniform distribution.
The two-outcome case Shannon plots in Fig. 7; it peaks at 1 bit when $p = q = 1/2$.

explorations.title: Certainty gives zero bits
explorations.change: Set the preset to **certain** (or drag $w_1$ to 1 and the rest to 0).
explorations.observe: The left chart shows one bar of height 1 and three of height 0. Every contribution bar in the right chart has height 0, and the total $H$ reads 0 bits.
explorations.why: When one $p_i = 1$ the outcome is known in advance, so there is no choice to measure. Formally $-1 \cdot \log_2 1 = 0$ and the zero-probability terms are defined as 0, so the whole sum is 0 — Shannon's Property (1).

explorations.title: Uniform distributions give $\log_2 n$ bits
explorations.change: Start at $n = 4$ with the uniform preset, then change $n$ to 2, then to 3, then to 6 (re-choosing the uniform preset each time).
explorations.observe: The total $H$ and the dashed reference line both move: $n=2$ gives 1 bit, $n=4$ gives 2 bits, $n=6$ gives about 2.585 bits. The 'uniform reference $\log_2 n$' readout always equals the total $H$ when the bars are level.
explorations.why: For equal probabilities each term is $-(1/n)\log_2(1/n) = (\log_2 n)/n$, and summing $n$ of them gives $\log_2 n$. This is Shannon's Property (2): more equally likely events means more uncertainty, and the growth is logarithmic, so doubling $n$ adds exactly one bit.

pitfall.title: Entropy is not the number of outcomes
pitfall.text: A distribution over 6 outcomes can have less entropy than one over 2 outcomes: if the 6-outcome distribution is very peaked, $H$ can be near 0, while two equally likely outcomes give exactly 1 bit. Entropy measures how **spread out** the probability mass is, not how many outcomes exist. The maximum $\log_2 n$ is only reached in the uniform case.

grounding.paper: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (C. E. Shannon, 1948)
grounding.section: Section 6, Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy (Theorem 2 and Properties (1)-(2))
from_source: Shannon considers a set of possible events with known probabilities $p_1, \dots, p_n$ and asks for a measure $H(p_1, \dots, p_n)$ of how much choice or uncertainty is involved.

He requires: (1) $H$ is continuous in the $p_i$; (2) if all $p_i$ are equal then $H$ is a monotonic increasing function of $n$; (3) breaking a choice into two successive choices makes the original $H$ the weighted sum of the individual values.
Theorem 2: the only $H$ satisfying these assumptions is $H = -K \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log p_i$, with $K$ a positive constant amounting to a choice of unit.
With logarithms to base 2 the unit is the bit.
Property (1): $H = 0$ if and only if all $p_i$ but one are zero, that one having the value unity; only when the outcome is certain does $H$ vanish, otherwise $H$ is positive.
Property (2): for a given $n$, $H$ is a maximum equal to $\log n$ when all $p_i$ are equal to $1/n$, which is also intuitively the most uncertain situation.
For two possibilities with probabilities $p$ and $q = 1-p$, $H = -(p \log p + q \log q)$, plotted as a function of $p$ in Fig. 7.
our_additions: The interactive playground, the weight-normalization step (entering arbitrary non-negative $w_i$ and dividing by their sum), and the choice of base-2 logs with $K=1$.
The convention $0 \log_2 0 = 0$ used to handle zero probabilities numerically.
The specific toy values in the presets and tests (e.g. $n=4$ uniform, the skewed distribution).
The bar-chart visual, the contribution decomposition $-p_i \log_2 p_i$, and the framing of entropy as 'how spread out the mass is'.
grounding.disclaimer: This page is a toy illustration of the entropy formula and its two stated properties. It does not reproduce Shannon's experiments or any coding results; all numbers shown come from evaluating $H = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i$ on the distribution you set.
